abstract: >-
  Most EEG source imaging methods assume brain activity arises from independent, focal sources and are validated mainly on their ability to localize a single generator, overlooking the brain's network structure and the co-activation of regions along it. We introduce weighted Connectome Spectrum Electromagnetic Tomography (wCSET), which replaces its predecessor CSET's L1 sparsity prior with a smooth, exponentially weighted L2 prior over the connectome-harmonic spectrum. We validate wCSET, CSET, three standard connectivity-agnostic methods, and a geometry-based (Laplace-Beltrami) alternative across three complementary studies that probe source reconstruction beyond localization. The first simulates activity propagating across a structural connectome, providing an exact network-level ground truth. The second uses a clinical cohort of 26 seizure-free patients with epilepsy, with the resected volume as ground truth. The third uses simultaneous scalp and intracranial EEG recordings, a rare direct electrophysiological benchmark. In simulation, wCSET matched standard methods at localizing a source's onset but substantially outperformed them at reconstructing the distributed co-activation patterns that follow as activity spreads, an advantage robust to moderate noise and to considerable connectome corruption. In the resection cohort, wCSET's localization did not differ significantly from any other method. Against intracranial recordings, wCSET outperformed the standard methods and CSET in one of two evaluable subjects on two polarity-invariant measures, and did not differ from them in the other. A purely geometric alternative matched wCSET's own performance throughout, suggesting cortical geometry alone may capture much of what drives accurate distributed reconstruction. Together, these results establish wCSET as a principled step beyond localization-only source imaging, and introduce a validation framework for evaluating such methods against a source's full co-activation pattern rather than its location alone.

# Introduction {#sec-introduction}

Electroencephalography (EEG) offers unparalleled temporal resolution for studying neural dynamics _in vivo_, but scalp EEG recordings pay for it in spatial resolution [@nunez_electric_2006]. Source reconstruction recovers some of that lost precision through minimum norm estimates (MNE), which project the EEG signal onto a cortical surface modeled from the individual's own MRI [@hamalainen_interpreting_1994; @dale_improved_1993].

Three decades of variants followed, including sLORETA [@pascual-marqui_standardized_2002], eLORETA [@pascual-marqui_discrete_2007] and dSPM [@dale_dynamic_2000], but the goal barely changed: pinpoint the isolated region behind a signal, a practice known as source localization [@knosche_eegmeg_2022]. Connectivity approaches now treat the brain as an integrated network rather than a set of independent regions [@bressler_large-scale_2010], and localization-focused methods are increasingly out of step with that view.

This gap is technical, not just conceptual: these methods assume independent sources, a prior known to underperform one informed by the true source covariance [@wipf_unified_2009]. The off-diagonal terms of that covariance encode which regions are active together; ignoring them is defensible when activity is genuinely focal, but not once multiple regions are co-active. Others report that incorporating the source covariance also helps with leakage (or field spread), a well-known problem in EEG source reconstruction [@schoffelen_source_2009; @gonzalez-moreira_caulking_2018].

Several strategies try to close that gap. The earliest, smoothness priors such as LORETA [@pascual-marqui_low_1994] and LAURA [@grave_de_peralta_menendez_noninvasive_2001], already impose a non-diagonal source covariance, but one fixed by local geometry rather than informed by how regions actually interact. Functional priors from fMRI can constrain expected interactions [@liu_fmri-si-stbf_2021], though fMRI's hemodynamic response unfolds over seconds, too slow to meaningfully constrain millisecond-scale EEG dynamics. Data-driven approaches instead jointly estimate source activity and its covariance structure from the recordings themselves, at the cost of greater ill-posedness and computation (e.g., BC-VARETA [@gonzalez-moreira_third_2018]). A final strategy leans on structure–function coupling directly: since neural activity propagates along the brain's structural scaffolding, the connectome estimated from diffusion MRI tractography offers a principled, subject-specific prior instead [@ruequeralt_connectome_2024].

Graph Signal Processing (GSP) supplies the machinery for this coupling [@shuman_emerging_2013]. Eigendecomposing the connectome's graph Laplacian yields brain harmonics ordered by graph frequency: low frequencies capture smooth, globally integrated activity, high frequencies more locally segregated patterns [@shuman_emerging_2013; @atasoy_human_2016]. Each harmonic is a spatial pattern of co-activation across regions, so reconstructing activity in this basis amounts to reconstructing co-activation patterns. Projecting source activity onto this basis (the Graph Fourier Transform, @sec-connectome) yields a compact "connectome spectrum," since both fMRI and EEG source activity concentrate their energy in a handful of low-frequency harmonics [@rue-queralt_connectome_2021; @atasoy_human_2016]. @ruequeralt_connectome_2024 built on this: Connectome Spectrum Electromagnetic Tomography (CSET) enforces an L₁ sparsity prior in this spectrum, restricting solutions to a small number of active harmonics.

A parallel line of work asks whether geometry alone can do the job. Substituting the Beltrami-Laplace operator on the cortical mesh for the connectome's graph Laplacian trades long-range white-matter pathways for fine-grained local geometry [@pang_geometric_2023]. @wang_geometry_2026 applied this idea to EEG/MEG source reconstruction with Geometric Basis Functions (GBF): whole-brain activity as a combination of the leading ~300 such eigenmodes under a logarithmically-decaying L₂ penalty. @siu_structural_2026 took a different route to the same source-reconstruction problem, using weighted Beltrami harmonics as a hard post-hoc spectral filter rather than a continuous penalty.

Unlike the geometry-based methods above, which weight low-order harmonics preferentially by construction, CSET does not weight its harmonics at all, which prevents it from separating biologically meaningful ones from noise-dominated ones. We close that gap with weighted CSET (wCSET): a weighted L₂ prior that decays exponentially with graph frequency, replacing CSET's L₁ prior with a continuous, eigenvalue-graded penalty in GBF's spirit, but applied to the connectome's graph Laplacian, retaining the white-matter awareness the geometry-based methods lack. The weighting is not arbitrary: @abdelnour_functional_2018 show that functional connectivity's eigenvalues relate to the structural Laplacian's via an approximately exponential mapping, so a small number of low-frequency structural eigenmodes already dominate functional connectivity.

Despite this progression toward increasingly principled spectral weightings, validation has not kept pace. @ruequeralt_connectome_2024 validated CSET by correlating reconstructed activity with fMRI from the same task, but fMRI's hemodynamic response reflects neural activity only indirectly and with substantial temporal blurring, making it a weak proxy for the electrophysiological ground truth these methods aim to reconstruct. Other works validate through source localization in epilepsy patients instead. Even where source extent improves, this criterion is misaligned with what connectivity-informed methods are designed to capture. These methods target the co-activation patterns across interconnected networks, not a focal source's spatial footprint, and localization accuracy does not measure such patterns. We hypothesize that connectivity-informed methods localize a source's onset about as well as standard methods, since activity is still focal at that point. Once activity spreads, however, they should reconstruct the resulting co-activation patterns more accurately. A localization benchmark alone would miss that advantage.

The primary barrier to a more appropriate validation is that no single benchmark provides a complete ground truth for network-level co-activation: simulations are exact but idealized, resections are clinically grounded but spatially coarse, and intracranial recordings are direct but sparsely sampled. We therefore combine three complementary fronts (@fig-overview), evaluating CSET and wCSET on each:

- **Study I:** We simulate activity propagating across the structural connectome itself (@sec-data-synthetic), giving an exact, fully known ground truth for network-level co-activation that no empirical recording can offer. We test whether connectivity-informed methods reconstruct the co-activation patterns that follow a source's onset, and how robust they are to erroneous connectivity data.

- **Study II:** In a clinical epilepsy cohort, the resected epileptogenic zone serves as ground truth, with post-surgical success confirming it truly contained the source. We test whether connectivity-informed methods localize it as accurately as standard methods.

- **Study III:** We revive and extend the framework of @grova_intracranial_2016 [see also @afnan_assessing_2026] correlating MEG and intracranial EEG (iEEG), extending it to truly simultaneous EEG/iEEG recordings, the only electrophysiological ground truth free from neurovascular coupling, skull attenuation, and temporal blurring [@nunez_electric_2006]. Projecting EEG-reconstructed sources onto iEEG electrode locations allows direct comparison of reconstructed and recorded co-activation patterns, via spatial correlation computed at each time point.

Together, these studies form a multi-level validation framework that moves source imaging beyond localization as its sole benchmark.


# Materials and Methods

Three complementary studies validate wCSET (@fig-overview). All three reconstruct the EEG with the same pipeline and the same six methods: three standard connectivity-agnostic baselines (wMNE, dSPM, sLORETA), two connectivity-informed methods (CSET, wCSET), and one geometry-based method (GBF). This section therefore first describes the shared pipeline (@sec-pipeline), then the datasets with their study-specific settings (@sec-datasets), then the metrics that compare the reconstructions with each study's ground truth (@sec-metrics), and finally the statistical analysis (@sec-stats).

![**Source reconstruction pipeline and the three validation studies.** All studies share one pipeline (top): MRI and electrode positions define the source space and forward model, the structural connectome provides the graph harmonics, and six inverse methods yield a reconstructed activity map. Red denotes brain activity and green denotes ground truth. **Study I (left):** activity is simulated as spreading across the structural connectome from a focal source, and the averaged EEG is reconstructed. Each method's map is compared with the ground truth by spatial correlation at each time point, shown for a single example at onset (t₁) and after spread (t₂) for wCSET and sLORETA only (the same example is shown in more detail in @sec-s1-localization); localization of the onset is evaluated separately (@sec-metric-loc). **Study II (middle):** in patients who were seizure-free after surgery, the location of maximal reconstructed activity is compared with the resection volume, measured as the Euclidean distance (0 mm if inside). **Study III (right):** EEG-reconstructed sources are projected onto the iEEG electrode positions ("virtual iEEG") and compared with the recorded iEEG (ground truth) at each time point, by signed spatial correlation and by a sign-free spatial overlap (AUC) across contacts.](results/overview_method.png){#fig-overview fig-alt="Schematic of the shared source reconstruction pipeline (MRI and electrode positions, source space, forward model, connectome and harmonics, inverse solution, reconstructed activity) branching into three study panels: simulation with ground-truth and reconstructed brain maps at two time points, resection cohort with the distance between estimated location and resection volume, and simultaneous EEG/iEEG with reconstructed sources projected onto intracranial electrodes."}

## Source Reconstruction Pipeline {#sec-pipeline}

### Source Space {#sec-source-space}

Neural activity was modeled using a distributed dipole model with a cortical constraint: the source space restricted to the cortical white matter surface, reconstructed from T1-weighted MRI using FreeSurfer (v.7.4.1), with 7,275–7,653 dipoles uniformly distributed across it via MNE-Python [@gramfort_meg_2013] at ~3.3 mm average spacing, orientations fixed normal to the cortical manifold (full subdivision scheme, tool versions, and orientation-constraint rationale in Annex).

### Volume Conduction Model {#sec-bem}

Volume conduction was modeled with a Boundary Element Model (BEM) [@hamalainen_realistic_1989] using MNE-Python's default conductivities (0.3 S/m brain/scalp, 0.006 S/m skull). We built the head model with a custom SimNIBS CHARM-based pipeline [@puonti_accurate_2020], fitting inner skull, outer skull, and scalp surfaces sequentially and non-intersecting (full pipeline and BEM comparison in Annex). In the clinical studies (@sec-data-resection, @sec-data-ieeg), EEG sensors were pre-co-registered to the T1-weighted MRI and thus intrinsically aligned with the head model; in the simulation (@sec-data-synthetic), the template EEG montage was projected onto the skin surface of the BEM. The forward solution (gain matrix) was computed via MNE-Python.

### Connectivity Matrices {#sec-connectome}

The brain is modeled as a graph (connectome) whose nodes are the source-space dipoles and whose edges represent physical anatomical links between them. The empirical connectome is available only for Study I's VEPCON subject; Studies II and III, lacking diffusion MRI, use the atlas surrogate below (@sec-data-resection, @sec-data-ieeg).

**Empirical connectomes**

Two types of structural links are incorporated: long-range connections from dMRI tractography, and short-range connections linking each dipole to its geodesically nearest neighbors, capturing local gray matter connectivity missed by standard tractography (thresholds in Annex); edges are weighted by distance (fiber length for long-range, geodesic distance for local).

**Connectome surrogates**

Where diffusion data is unavailable, we evaluate three connectome surrogates, validated via our simulation framework (@sec-study1) and summarized in @tbl-surrogates; two are also tested in binarized form (edge presence only) to isolate topology from edge-weight fidelity, yielding five variants in total. The atlas surrogate relies on the multi-scale connectivity (MultiConn) atlas [@aleman-gomez_multi-scale_2022], a probabilistic population atlas of the human structural connectome, used at scale 4.

| Surrogate | Construction | Binarized variant? | Tests whether... |
|:---|:---|:---:|:---|
| Atlas | Long-range tracts from the MultiConn atlas's [@aleman-gomez_multi-scale_2022] reference population, plus gray matter connections as above (Annex) | Yes | A population atlas can substitute for subject-specific tractography |
| Local | Gray matter connectivity only, plus homotopic cross-hemisphere links to keep the graph connected (Annex) | Yes | Local geometry alone, without long-range information, suffices |
| Beltrami-operator | Laplace-Beltrami eigenmodes of the cortical mesh directly [@pang_geometric_2023]; no explicit connectome graph is built (Annex) | No (purest geometry-only control) | Cortical geometry alone suffices |

: Connectome surrogates. {#tbl-surrogates}

**Graph Fourier Transform**

Edge weights are distances, so we invert them to obtain an adjacency matrix $\mathbf A$ that describes connection strength. This is consistent with the approximately exponential decay of connectivity strength with distance [@ercsey-ravasz_predictive_2013]: shorter, more direct connections couple more strongly. From $\mathbf A$, we build the normalized graph Laplacian $\mathcal L = \mathbf I - \mathbf D^{-1/2}\mathbf A\mathbf D^{-1/2}$, where $\mathbf D$ is the degree matrix, the operator underlying Graph Signal Processing (GSP) on neural data [@shuman_emerging_2013; @ortega_graph_2018].

The eigendecomposition of $\mathcal L$ defines the Graph Fourier Transform (GFT):

$$
\mathcal L = \mathbf{U}\mathbf{\Lambda}\mathbf{U}^\top
$$

Here the columns of $\mathbf{U} = [u_1, u_2, \ldots, u_N]$ are the eigenvectors of $\mathcal L$, which we call graph harmonics, and $\mathbf{\Lambda}$ contains the corresponding eigenvalues, their graph frequencies. The GFT expresses brain activity in this harmonic basis. For GBF, the Laplace-Beltrami operator of the cortical mesh replaces $\mathcal L$, and its eigenmodes replace $\mathbf U$.

### Inverse Problem and Methods {#sec-inverse}

Every study used MNE-Python's wMNE [@hamalainen_interpreting_1994], dSPM [@dale_dynamic_2000], and sLORETA [@pascual-marqui_standardized_2002] as standard baselines against two connectivity-informed methods, CSET and wCSET, and one geometry-based method, GBF. All methods were whitened using an empirically estimated noise covariance [@dale_dynamic_2000; @knosche_eegmeg_2022] (exception: Study II, see @sec-data-resection).

**General formulation.** We estimate dipole activities $\mathbf s\in \mathbb R^n$ from sensor measurements $\mathbf y \in \mathbb R^m$ via the forward model $\mathbf y = \mathbf L \mathbf s + \epsilon$, where $\mathbf L$ is the lead-field matrix; because $n\gg m$, the problem is ill-posed. The Maximum A Posteriori (MAP) estimate is the regularized least-squares problem:

$$
\mathbf s^* = \text{arg }\underset{\mathbf s}{\text{min}}\underbrace{\lVert\mathbf y-\mathbf L\mathbf s\rVert_2^2}_{\text{Data Fidelity}} + \lambda\underbrace{\lVert \mathbf C \mathbf s\rVert_p^p}_{\text{Regularization}} \tag{1}
$$

Here $\lambda$ balances data fit against the prior (@sec-lambda), and $\mathbf C$ encodes the prior. For $p=2$, the prior is Gaussian with source covariance $\mathbf\Sigma_{\mathbf s}=(\mathbf C^\top\mathbf C)^{-1}$.

**Solvers.** For $p=1$, the solution is sparse; it has no closed form and is solved via proximal gradient descent. For $p=2$, the solution is analytic. Writing $\mathbf\Sigma_{\mathbf s}=\mathbf B\mathbf B^\top$ and decomposing $\mathbf L\mathbf B=\mathbf E_f\mathbf\Gamma\mathbf E_\ell^\top$ by singular value decomposition (singular values $\gamma_k$), it is computed as in MNE-Python [@gramfort_meg_2013]:

$$
\mathbf s^*=\mathbf B\,\mathbf E_\ell\,\mathbf D_\lambda\,\mathbf E_f^\top\mathbf y,\qquad \mathbf D_\lambda=\mathrm{diag}\!\left(\frac{\gamma_k}{\gamma_k^2+\lambda}\right) \tag{2}
$$

**Connectivity-agnostic priors.** sLORETA and dSPM use $\mathbf C=\mathbf I$ and $p=2$, then standardize the solution post hoc (Annex). wMNE uses $p=2$ and $\mathbf C=\mathbf W_d^{-1}$, where the depth-weighting matrix $W_{d,ii}=\lVert\mathbf L_{:i}\rVert^{-\kappa}$ ($\kappa=0.8$) counteracts the bias toward superficial dipoles. In all three, $\mathbf C$, and hence $\mathbf\Sigma_{\mathbf s}$, is diagonal: every pair of sources is uncorrelated a priori, and depth weighting only changes their variances. Nothing in the prior encodes which regions co-activate, which is why we call these methods connectivity-agnostic.

**Connectivity-informed priors.** CSET and wCSET penalize the depth-weighted source activity in the connectome spectrum, $\mathbf U^\top\mathbf W_d^{-1}\mathbf s$ ($\kappa=0.2$, tuned in simulation, @sec-study1). $\mathbf C$ is then no longer diagonal: the connectome harmonics couple the sources. Since the connectome spectrum is compact, CSET [@ruequeralt_connectome_2024] uses a sparse prior ($p=1$):

$$
\mathbf s^* = \text{arg }\underset{\mathbf s}{\text{min}}\lVert\mathbf y-\mathbf L\mathbf s\rVert_2^2 + \lambda\lVert \mathbf U^\top\mathbf W_d^{-1}\mathbf s\rVert_1 \tag{3}
$$

wCSET adds harmonic weights that follow an exponential low-pass filter on graph frequency, $W_{h,ii} = \exp(-\beta\lambda_i)$ ($\lambda_i$: eigenvalue of harmonic $i$, in $[0, 2]$; $\beta = 5$, tuned in simulation), and uses a smooth prior ($p=2$):

$$
\mathbf s^* = \text{arg }\underset{\mathbf s}{\text{min}}\lVert\mathbf y-\mathbf L\mathbf s\rVert_2^2 + \lambda\lVert \mathbf W_h^{-1}\mathbf U^\top\mathbf W_d^{-1}\mathbf s\rVert_2^2 \tag{4}
$$

High graph frequencies are thus penalized most, and $\mathbf\Sigma_{\mathbf s}=\mathbf W_d\mathbf U\mathbf W_h^2\mathbf U^\top\mathbf W_d$. The solution is Eq. (2) with $\mathbf B=\mathbf W_d\mathbf U\mathbf W_h$.

**Geometry-based prior.** GBF [@wang_geometry_2026] is implemented as wCSET with three substitutions: the Laplace-Beltrami eigenmodes of the cortical mesh $\mathbf U_{\text{LB}}$ replace $\mathbf U$ (@sec-connectome), $\mathbf W_d=\mathbf I$, and $\mathbf W_h$ becomes GBF's hard-truncated, log-form weighting (cutoff $S=150$; formula and tuning in Annex). Its solution is Eq. (2) with $\mathbf B=\mathbf U_{\text{LB}}\mathbf W_h$. It was tested in all three studies: as the Beltrami connectome surrogate in Study I (@sec-s1-surrogates), and alongside the other methods in Studies II and III (@sec-study2, @sec-study3).

### Regularization Parameter Selection {#sec-lambda}

For all methods except CSET, $\lambda$ is set per run from the evoked response's own estimated peak-amplitude SNR rather than fixed a priori, following MNE-Python's convention $\lambda = 1/\text{SNR}^2$, floored at $\lambda = \max(0.01, 1/\text{SNR}^2)$ so regularization doesn't vanish at high SNR. CSET is the exception: its $\lambda$ is instead fixed at $0.1$, tuned once against reconstruction accuracy in simulation (@sec-study1) rather than re-estimated per run.

## Datasets and Study-Specific Settings {#sec-datasets}

### Synthetic Data {#sec-data-synthetic}

Simulations used anatomical data from a single representative VEPCON subject [@pascucci_source_2022]: a T1-weighted MRI and a tractogram derived from diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI). The tractogram was reconstructed with constrained spherical deconvolution (CSD) and deterministic streamline tractography. EEG was simulated on the 204-channel montage used throughout (@sec-data-resection). The cortical source space (@sec-source-space) was parcellated into 446 regions, using the same cortical parcellation as scale 4 of the MultiConn atlas (@sec-connectome). From these, 100 regions were selected via farthest-point sampling as a spatially uniform probe set, reused throughout. The only exception is the noise-robustness analysis (@sec-s1-data-noise), which uses a separate, independently sampled 50-region subset. This subset was kept smaller because the analysis sweeps multiple SNR levels per region.

In each trial, a source region drawn from the probe set was assigned a 50 ms double-Hanning-window spike waveform [@dewouters_source-reconstructed_2026] (mimicking a clinical interictal spike) on all its dipoles. This follows approaches modelling epileptiform activity as a patch of simultaneously active dipoles rather than a point source [@afnan_eegmeg_2024]. The spike repeated every 1 s across a 20 s recording; after propagation and sensor projection (below and @sec-bem), the 20 resulting events were epoched and averaged into a single evoked response per run.

**Propagation model.** Activity was propagated across the connectome in a feedforward manner, with each dipole's activity a delayed and spatially-decayed copy of the source waveform:

$$
S_j(t) = \gamma^{h_j} \cdot s_0\!\left(t - \tau_j\right)
$$

where $h_j$ is the hop count from source to dipole $j$, $\gamma = 0.5$ is a per-hop spatial decay factor, and $\tau_j$ is a propagation delay based on conduction speed, nodal delay, and timing jitter (full model in Annex).

**Noise model.** Pink noise (source level) and white noise (sensor level) were calibrated to a literature-typical 15 µV RMS baseline [@nunez_electric_2006] and a single-trial SNR of 5 (parameter values in Annex Table 3; derivation also in the Annex).

Each simulation was repeated 8 times per source region; region/repetition counts were set via a power analysis for the region-paired comparisons reported in Results (full analysis in Annex).

**Inverse crime.** For Study I only, a second forward solution used a deliberately mismatched skull conductivity (0.012 S/m) to avoid the inverse crime [@wirgin_inverse_2004]. The two models differ by approximately 10% (Annex).

**Connectome perturbation.** To test robustness to imperfect connectome knowledge, we perturb the connectome before source reconstruction (@sec-s1-prior-noise). Perturbation uses a degree-preserving double-edge swap (two random edges re-paired, degree unchanged), at severities from 0–100% of total edges.

**Preprocessing.** The epochs were processed with a Common Average Reference [@bertrand_theoretical_1985], baseline correction, and noise-covariance estimation from the pre-spike period before averaging.

### Clinical Dataset A: Resection Cohort {#sec-data-resection}

We used the dataset of @vorderwulbecke_high-density_2025 to validate EEG source localization clinically. It comprises 44 patients with pharmacoresistant focal epilepsy who underwent resective surgery. Surgical outcome was graded on the ILAE scale at 12 months (1 = seizure-free, 2–6 = increasing persistent seizures). We restricted analysis to seizure-free outcomes (ILAE 1, 28 patients). In patients with residual seizures, the resection may not fully encompass the true epileptogenic zone, which makes it an unreliable ground truth. We excluded two further patients: one had no genuine resection cavity, and the other lacked the EEG channel locations needed for coregistration. The remaining 26 patients each had a pre- and post-operative T1-weighted MRI and a pre-operative interictal EEG recording (resection masks are described below). Epileptic spikes had been visually identified by clinical experts among the dataset's authors, then averaged time-locked to their peak. The dataset's 257-channel EEG (HydroCel Geodesic Sensor Net) was reduced to the 204-channel montage used throughout by excluding cheek electrodes. As individual diffusion MRI was unavailable, the structural connectome was instead derived from the population probabilistic tractography atlas (@sec-connectome).

**Preprocessing.** EEG arrived as pre-averaged spikes, already filtered, downsampled, and interpolated by the data providers (@vorderwulbecke_high-density_2025; parameters in Annex); without individual epochs, noise-covariance estimation was not possible and an ad-hoc identity covariance was used instead (no whitening). A Common Average Reference, a notch filter for residual 50 Hz noise, and baseline correction were applied where needed.

**Ground truth.** Ground-truth brain activity maps are not directly available clinically, so we use the resected area, since these patients were seizure-free after surgery, marking their resection as containing the epileptogenic zone.

**Resection mask segmentation.** Resection masks were generated with RAMPS [@simpson_automated_2025], which estimates resected volume from pre-/post-operative T1-weighted MRI. RAMPS also requires the resection's hemisphere and lobe as input, which we identified visually on the post-operative T1-weighted MRI. Masks were then visually inspected for quality (by overlaying pre-/post-operative T1w and mask), with manual segmentation used to replace unusable automated masks.

### Clinical Dataset B: Simultaneous EEG/iEEG Cohort {#sec-data-ieeg}

To validate source reconstruction against ground-truth intracranial activity, we used a cohort of 4 patients with simultaneously recorded scalp EEG and intracranial EEG (iEEG).

Epileptic spikes were identified and epoched in both modalities, time-locked to the same events, yielding paired scalp/intracranial recordings of the same underlying activity. Spikes were visually identified and marked on iEEG, cross-validated using Delphos, an automated spike detector [@roehri_time-frequency_2016; @roehri_assets_2017], following the same acquisition and marking protocol used for this cohort by @roehri_scalp-negative_2025. Each patient's T1-weighted MRI was processed identically to the resection cohort (Clinical Dataset A) for anatomical/forward modeling (@sec-pipeline), and the structural connectome was derived the same way (individual diffusion MRI was likewise unavailable). Results are reported in the main text for two of the four subjects. In the other two, the spikes originated from deep sources, far from the cortical mesh on which activity is reconstructed (@sec-source-space). Projecting the reconstructed activity onto the virtual iEEG contacts near these deep sources is therefore unreliable, so their results appear in the Annex instead.

**Preprocessing.** EEG epochs were processed as in Study I and averaged into the evoked response (130–265 marked spikes per subject).

**Ground truth.** iEEG epochs were averaged directly into the ground-truth evoked response, with no further preprocessing. Because intracranial recordings sample the potential only at sparse contacts, reconstructed cortical activity was projected onto these contacts as "virtual" iEEG, following @grova_intracranial_2016 and @afnan_assessing_2026: each dipole's potential at a contact is computed in an infinite homogeneous conductor, then summed over dipoles. Source-contact distances below 3 mm, the assumed iEEG-MRI coregistration accuracy, are set to 3 mm to avoid instabilities near the source.

**Comparison window.** Virtual and recorded iEEG were compared only over the part of the epoch where the recorded signal is stronger than during the baseline. This window was detected per subject with an adaptive threshold on the global field power of the recorded iEEG relative to its baseline (criterion in Annex), whereas @grova_intracranial_2016 used a fixed number of samples around the spike peak.

## Performance Evaluation Metrics {#sec-metrics}

Each study compares reconstructions with its ground truth using one or two of three metrics (@tbl-metrics), each defined once below.

| Metric | Study I (simulation) | Study II (resection) | Study III (EEG/iEEG) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Localization error | quarter rising phase | half rising phase | — |
| Spatial correlation | across dipoles, over time | — | across contacts (rank of absolute amplitude), over time |
| Spatial overlap (AUC) | — | — | across contacts, over time |

: Metrics used in each study. {#tbl-metrics}

### Localization Accuracy {#sec-metric-loc}

Localization was evaluated on the spike's rising phase, balancing little spread early against higher SNR later, rather than at the peak, by which the source has typically spread. For the simulation, we used 25% of the rising phase (quarter rising phase, qrp), where the source is still focal. For the resection cohort, we used 50% (half rising phase, hrp), which @vorderwulbecke_high-density_2020 found most accurate on this dataset. Localization error is the Euclidean distance from the location of maximal source activity to the boundary of the target mask (the seed region in simulation, the resection volume in the cohort), set to 0 mm if that location lies inside it [@wang_geometry_2026].

### Spatial Correlation {#sec-metric-corr}

Reconstructions were compared with ground truth via spatial correlation at each time point. In Study I, it was the Pearson correlation across dipoles between reconstructed and simulated activity maps. In Study III, it was computed across intracranial contacts between the virtual iEEG and the recorded iEEG (@sec-data-ieeg). The polarity of intracranial recordings is difficult to interpret, as it depends on each contact's position relative to the generator and on the reference. We therefore compared only the absolute amplitudes, using the Spearman rank correlation. Because it compares ranks, this measure is also insensitive to the different amplitude scales of virtual and recorded iEEG. For comparison with @grova_intracranial_2016 and @afnan_assessing_2026, who report the signed Pearson correlation, the Annex also reports that measure. Unlike these studies, which compared virtual and recorded iEEG at the spike peak only, we computed every measure at each time point of a comparison window (@sec-data-ieeg).
### Spatial Overlap {#sec-metric-auc}

In Study III, we complemented the spatial correlation with a measure of spatial overlap that ignores each contact's polarity: the area under the ROC curve (AUC) [@grova_evaluation_2006; @afnan_assessing_2026]. At each time point, contacts whose recorded absolute amplitude reached at least 30% of that time point's maximum were labelled active, as in @afnan_assessing_2026. The AUC is the probability that the virtual iEEG's absolute amplitude is larger at an active contact than at an inactive one (0.5 = chance, 1 = perfect separation). Like the spatial correlation, it was computed at every time point of the comparison window.

## Statistical Analysis {#sec-stats}

### Chance Level {#sec-metric-chance}

For the signed spatial correlation reported in the Annex, chance levels were estimated following @afnan_assessing_2026, by randomly permuting the contact labels of the virtual iEEG (1000 permutations, recomputing the correlation at every time point) and taking the 2.5–97.5th percentiles of the resulting null distribution.

### Method Comparisons {#sec-stats-tests}

Method comparisons are paired and tested against a reference method, typically wCSET. Pairing is by region in simulation, by subject in the resection cohort, and by timepoint in the EEG/iEEG cohort. Single-value outcomes, such as localization error, were compared with the Wilcoxon signed-rank test (rank-biserial effect size). In Study III, successive timepoints are autocorrelated, so we used a paired t-test with an autocorrelation-corrected effective sample size instead (Cohen's dz; derivation in Annex). Outcomes along a continuous coordinate (SNR, time, perturbation severity) were compared with cluster-based permutation testing (procedure in Annex). All p-values were Benjamini-Hochberg FDR-corrected within their comparison family (α = 0.05).

## Study I: Simulation-Based Validation {#sec-study1}

### Localization vs. Propagation {#sec-s1-localization}

```{python filename="simf_localization_stats.py"}
#| output: false
import mindmap as mm

simf_metrics = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load("./results/simf/flagship")
competitors = [m for m in METHODS if m != "wcset"]

# Localization error at qrp: wCSET vs. each competitor, paired by region.
loc1_results = simf_metrics.stat.wilcoxon(
    "localization_error", group_by="Method",
    comparisons=simf_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(["wcset"], competitors), pairing_col="region",
    filters={"phase": "qrp"},
)

# Statistics quoted in the prose.
# Effect as stored is wCSET - competitor (positive = wCSET's error is larger); flipped so that
# positive = wCSET better, as in the figure.
_loc1 = loc1_results.vs("wcset")
loc1_sloreta_p = fmt_p(_loc1.loc["sloreta", "p_corrected"], thresh=0.0001)
loc1_sloreta_r = fmt_stat(-_loc1.loc["sloreta", "effect"])
loc1_dspm_p = fmt_p(_loc1.loc["dspm", "p_corrected"])
loc1_dspm_r = fmt_stat(-_loc1.loc["dspm", "effect"])
loc1_wmne_p = fmt_p(_loc1.loc["wmne", "p_corrected"], thresh=0.0001)
loc1_wmne_r = fmt_stat(-_loc1.loc["wmne", "effect"])
loc1_cset_p = fmt_p(_loc1.loc["cset", "p_corrected"])
loc1_cset_r = fmt_stat(-_loc1.loc["cset", "effect"])
loc1_p_max = fmt_p(_loc1["p_corrected"].max())

# Spatial correlation over time: cluster permutation vs. wCSET, paired by region.
times_order = sorted(simf_metrics.to_df(metrics="correlation")["times"].unique())

corr1_results = simf_metrics.stat.cluster_permutation(
    "correlation", coord="times", group_by="Method",
    comparisons=simf_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(["wcset"], competitors), pairing_col="region",
    coord_order=times_order, higher_is_better=True,
    n_permutations=3000, seed=0,
)

# Statistics quoted in the prose: the largest cluster where wCSET is better (sign = +1), which spans
# the simulated spike. Clusters of the opposite sign fall in the baseline and after the spike, where
# the averaged EEG is noise only and the correlations are not interpretable.
def _better(competitor):
    clusters = corr1_results.clusters_by_pair[("wcset", competitor)]
    return main_cluster(clusters[clusters["sign"] == 1])

corr1_sloreta, corr1_dspm, corr1_wmne, corr1_cset = (_better(c) for c in ["sloreta", "dspm", "wmne", "cset"])

corr1_sloreta_p = fmt_p(corr1_sloreta["p_corrected"])
corr1_sloreta_dz = fmt_stat(corr1_sloreta["effect_size"])
corr1_dspm_p = fmt_p(corr1_dspm["p_corrected"])
corr1_dspm_dz = fmt_stat(corr1_dspm["effect_size"])
corr1_wmne_p = fmt_p(corr1_wmne["p_corrected"])
corr1_wmne_dz = fmt_stat(corr1_wmne["effect_size"])
corr1_cset_p = fmt_p(corr1_cset["p_corrected"])
corr1_cset_dz = fmt_stat(corr1_cset["effect_size"])
corr1_std_dz_lo = fmt_stat(min(c["effect_size"] for c in [corr1_sloreta, corr1_dspm, corr1_wmne]))
corr1_std_dz_hi = fmt_stat(max(c["effect_size"] for c in [corr1_sloreta, corr1_dspm, corr1_wmne]))
corr1_p_max = fmt_p(max(c["p_corrected"] for c in [corr1_sloreta, corr1_dspm, corr1_wmne, corr1_cset]))

# Window of the wCSET-better clusters (start rounded, so onset reads 0 ms; end varies by competitor).
_better_clusters = [corr1_sloreta, corr1_dspm, corr1_wmne, corr1_cset]
corr1_window_start = fmt_num(round(min(c["times_start"] for c in _better_clusters) * 1000), digits=0)
corr1_window_end_lo = fmt_num(min(c["times_end"] for c in _better_clusters) * 1000, digits=0)
corr1_window_end_hi = fmt_num(max(c["times_end"] for c in _better_clusters) * 1000, digits=0)

# Time of the largest gap between connectivity-informed and standard methods.
corr_collapsed = simf_metrics.to_df(metrics="correlation").groupby(
    ["Method", "region", "times"], as_index=False,
)["Value"].mean()
corr_median_curve = corr_collapsed.groupby(["Method", "times"], as_index=False)["Value"].median()
corr_pivot = corr_median_curve.pivot(index="times", columns="Method", values="Value").sort_index()
corr_gap = corr_pivot[["wcset", "cset"]].mean(axis=1) - corr_pivot[["sloreta", "dspm", "wmne"]].mean(axis=1)
corr1_gap_peak_time = fmt_num(corr_gap.idxmax() * 1000, digits=0)
```

We tested the hypothesis stated in @sec-introduction: connectivity-informed methods should localize a source's onset about as well as standard methods, but reconstruct the co-activation patterns that follow more accurately. We used the simulation described in @sec-data-synthetic, which produces complex, fully known ground-truth activity from a single known source (@fig-flagship-example). At the quarter rising phase (@sec-metric-loc), wCSET's localization error differed significantly from every other method's, in both directions (@fig-s1-localization a; Wilcoxon signed-rank vs. wCSET, region-paired, FDR-corrected, all p_corrected `{python} loc1_p_max`). Where wCSET was worse, the effects were small (rank-biserial r = `{python} loc1_cset_r` against CSET and `{python} loc1_dspm_r` against dSPM; positive = wCSET better). Where it was better, they were moderate to large (r = `{python} loc1_sloreta_r` against sLORETA and `{python} loc1_wmne_r` against wMNE).

wCSET's advantage emerged as activity spread from the source. Throughout the EEG spike, from onset (`{python} corr1_window_start` ms) until `{python} corr1_window_end_lo`–`{python} corr1_window_end_hi` ms depending on the method, wCSET's spatial correlation with the ground truth was significantly higher than every other method's (@fig-s1-localization b; cluster-based permutation, region-paired, FDR-corrected, all p_corrected `{python} corr1_p_max`). The effect was larger against the three standard methods (Cohen's dz = `{python} corr1_std_dz_lo`–`{python} corr1_std_dz_hi`) than against CSET (dz = `{python} corr1_cset_dz`), and the gap between connectivity-informed and standard methods was largest at `{python} corr1_gap_peak_time` ms, close to the peak phase. Before onset and after the EEG spike, the averaged EEG contains only noise, so every method's correlation stays near zero there and is not interpreted.




### Robustness to Data Noise {#sec-s1-data-noise}

```{python filename="simf_noise_summary_stats.py"}
#| output: false
import mindmap as mm

# Same tests as the Annex (cached): cluster permutation over SNR, wCSET vs. each competitor,
# region-paired. sign = +1 and positive dz = wCSET better.
noise_metrics = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load("./results/simf/noise_sweep")
competitors = [m for m in METHODS if m != "wcset"]
standard = ["sloreta", "dspm", "wmne"]

def _snr_order(metric):
    return sorted(noise_metrics.to_df(metrics=metric, filters={"phase": "qrp"})["snr"].unique(), reverse=True)

def _noise_test(metric, phase, higher_is_better):
    return noise_metrics.stat.cluster_permutation(
        metric, coord="snr", group_by="Method",
        comparisons=noise_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(["wcset"], competitors), pairing_col="region",
        coord_order=_snr_order(metric), higher_is_better=higher_is_better, filters={"phase": phase},
        n_permutations=3000, seed=0,
    )

def _cluster(clusters, sign):
    """Largest cluster of the given sign, or None if there is none."""
    rows = clusters[clusters["sign"] == sign] if not clusters.empty else clusters
    return None if rows.empty else main_cluster(rows)

noise_loc = _noise_test("localization_error", "qrp", higher_is_better=False)
noise_corr = {phase: _noise_test("correlation", phase, higher_is_better=True) for phase in ["qrp", "pp"]}

# Localization error: wCSET-better clusters per competitor (CSET: no cluster at all).
_loc = {c: _cluster(noise_loc.clusters_by_pair[("wcset", c)], 1) for c in competitors}
assert _loc["cset"] is None
noise_loc_wmne_dz, noise_loc_wmne_p = fmt_stat(_loc["wmne"]["effect_size"]), fmt_p(_loc["wmne"]["p_corrected"])
noise_loc_dspm_end, noise_loc_sloreta_end = fmt_num(_loc["dspm"]["snr_end"], 0), fmt_num(_loc["sloreta"]["snr_end"], 0)
noise_loc_dspm_dz, noise_loc_sloreta_dz = fmt_stat(_loc["dspm"]["effect_size"]), fmt_stat(_loc["sloreta"]["effect_size"])
noise_loc_dspm_p, noise_loc_sloreta_p = fmt_p(_loc["dspm"]["p_corrected"]), fmt_p(_loc["sloreta"]["p_corrected"])

# Spatial correlation, both phases: wCSET-better clusters down to some SNR, wCSET-worse clusters below it.
_better = {(ph, c): _cluster(noise_corr[ph].clusters_by_pair[("wcset", c)], 1) for ph in noise_corr for c in competitors}
_worse = {(ph, c): _cluster(noise_corr[ph].clusters_by_pair[("wcset", c)], -1) for ph in noise_corr for c in competitors}
noise_corr_end_std = fmt_num(max(_better[(ph, c)]["snr_end"] for ph in noise_corr for c in standard), 0)
noise_corr_end_cset = fmt_num(max(_better[(ph, "cset")]["snr_end"] for ph in noise_corr), 0)
noise_corr_dz_lo = fmt_stat(min(b["effect_size"] for b in _better.values()))
noise_corr_dz_hi = fmt_stat(max(b["effect_size"] for b in _better.values()))
noise_corr_p_max = fmt_p(max(b["p_corrected"] for b in _better.values()))
noise_corr_worse_p_max = f'{max(w["p_corrected"] for w in _worse.values() if w is not None):.3f}'
```

We swept the single-trial SNR from 20 down to 1 (@sec-data-synthetic). wCSET's spatial-correlation advantage held down to SNR `{python} noise_corr_end_std` against the standard methods and SNR `{python} noise_corr_end_cset` against CSET, at both the quarter rising phase and the peak (Annex Figure 6; cluster-based permutation, region-paired, FDR-corrected, all p_corrected `{python} noise_corr_p_max`, dz = `{python} noise_corr_dz_lo`–`{python} noise_corr_dz_hi`). Below that, every method's correlation fell close to zero and wCSET's was slightly lower (all p_corrected ≤ `{python} noise_corr_worse_p_max`), as the spike was no longer distinguishable from the noise.

Localization error rose for every method as SNR decreased (Annex Figure 5). wMNE degraded first, while the other four methods held until roughly SNR 3–5. wCSET was more accurate than wMNE across the whole range (dz = `{python} noise_loc_wmne_dz`, p_corrected `{python} noise_loc_wmne_p`), and more accurate than dSPM and sLORETA only at high SNR (down to SNR `{python} noise_loc_dspm_end` and `{python} noise_loc_sloreta_end`; dz = `{python} noise_loc_dspm_dz` and `{python} noise_loc_sloreta_dz`, p_corrected `{python} noise_loc_dspm_p` and `{python} noise_loc_sloreta_p`). It never differed significantly from CSET.

### Robustness to Prior Noise {#sec-s1-prior-noise}

```{python filename="simf_degradation_summary_stats.py"}
#| output: false
import mindmap as mm

deg_metrics_summary = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load("./results/simf/degradation")
_perm_d_summary = deg_metrics_summary.metadata["derived"]

# localization error (mm): wCSET's gradual rise vs. CSET's flat-then-sharp pattern
_loc_df_summary = deg_metrics_summary.to_df(metrics="localization_error", filters={"phase": "qrp"})
_loc_med_summary = _loc_df_summary.groupby(["Method", "percentage"])["Value"].median().unstack("percentage")

deg_summary_ref_loc_sloreta = fmt_num(_perm_d_summary["ref_loc"]["sloreta"])
deg_summary_loc_wcset_0 = fmt_num(_loc_med_summary.loc["wcset", 0])
deg_summary_loc_wcset_100 = fmt_num(_perm_d_summary["loc_wcset_100"])
deg_summary_loc_cset_lo_s = fmt_num(_loc_med_summary.loc["cset", 0:60].min())
deg_summary_loc_cset_hi_s = fmt_num(_loc_med_summary.loc["cset", 0:60].max())
deg_summary_loc_cset_100 = fmt_num(_loc_med_summary.loc["cset", 100])

# spatial correlation: wCSET's gradual decline vs. CSET's flat-then-sharp pattern
deg_summary_ref_corr_sloreta = fmt_num(_perm_d_summary["ref_corr"]["sloreta"], 2)
deg_summary_corr_wcset_0 = fmt_num(_perm_d_summary["corr_wcset_0"], 2)
deg_summary_corr_wcset_100 = fmt_num(_perm_d_summary["corr_wcset_100"], 2)
deg_summary_corr_cset_lo, deg_summary_corr_cset_hi = _perm_d_summary["corr_cset_0_60"]
deg_summary_corr_cset_lo_s = fmt_num(deg_summary_corr_cset_lo, 2)
deg_summary_corr_cset_hi_s = fmt_num(deg_summary_corr_cset_hi, 2)
deg_summary_corr_cset_100 = fmt_num(_perm_d_summary["corr_cset_100"], 2)

# Same tests as the Annex (cached): cluster permutation over perturbation level, CSET/wCSET vs. sLORETA,
# region-paired. sLORETA is the reference, so sign = -1 means CSET/wCSET is better; dz is flipped
# below so that positive = CSET/wCSET better, as in the other comparisons.
def _deg_test(metric, higher_is_better):
    order = sorted(deg_metrics_summary.to_df(metrics=metric, filters={"phase": "qrp"})["percentage"].unique())
    return deg_metrics_summary.stat.cluster_permutation(
        metric, coord="percentage", group_by="Method",
        comparisons=deg_metrics_summary.stat.build_comparisons(["sloreta"], ["cset", "wcset"]),
        pairing_col="region", coord_order=order, higher_is_better=higher_is_better, filters={"phase": "qrp"},
        n_permutations=3000, seed=0,
    )

_deg = {"loc": _deg_test("localization_error", higher_is_better=False), "corr": _deg_test("correlation", higher_is_better=True)}

def _deg_cluster(metric, method, better):
    clusters = _deg[metric].clusters_by_pair[("sloreta", method)]
    rows = clusters[clusters["sign"] == (-1 if better else 1)]
    return None if rows.empty else main_cluster(rows)

for _m in ["loc", "corr"]:
    for _method in ["cset", "wcset"]:
        _b, _w = _deg_cluster(_m, _method, True), _deg_cluster(_m, _method, False)
        globals()[f"deg_{_m}_{_method}_better_end"] = fmt_num(_b["percentage_end"], 0)
        globals()[f"deg_{_m}_{_method}_better_dz"] = fmt_stat(-_b["effect_size"])
        globals()[f"deg_{_m}_{_method}_better_p"] = fmt_p(_b["p_corrected"])
        if _w is not None:
            globals()[f"deg_{_m}_{_method}_worse_start"] = fmt_num(_w["percentage_start"], 0)
            globals()[f"deg_{_m}_{_method}_worse_dz"] = fmt_stat(-_w["effect_size"])
            globals()[f"deg_{_m}_{_method}_worse_p"] = fmt_p(_w["p_corrected"])
# wCSET never becomes significantly worse than sLORETA on localization error (no cluster of that sign).
assert _deg_cluster("loc", "wcset", False) is None
```

We perturbed an increasing share of the connectome's edges (@sec-data-synthetic) and compared CSET and wCSET with the connectome-agnostic sLORETA at the quarter rising phase (cluster-based permutation, region-paired, FDR-corrected; positive dz = CSET/wCSET better). wCSET degraded gradually and never became significantly worse than sLORETA, whereas CSET held up to moderate perturbation and then fell below it.

For localization error (Annex Figure 7), wCSET's error rose from `{python} deg_summary_loc_wcset_0` mm without perturbation to `{python} deg_summary_loc_wcset_100` mm at 100%, against `{python} deg_summary_ref_loc_sloreta` mm for sLORETA. It was significantly lower than sLORETA's up to `{python} deg_loc_wcset_better_end`% perturbation (dz = `{python} deg_loc_wcset_better_dz`, p_corrected `{python} deg_loc_wcset_better_p`), and never significantly higher. CSET's error stayed at `{python} deg_summary_loc_cset_lo_s`–`{python} deg_summary_loc_cset_hi_s` mm up to 60%, then rose to `{python} deg_summary_loc_cset_100` mm. It was lower than sLORETA's up to `{python} deg_loc_cset_better_end`% (dz = `{python} deg_loc_cset_better_dz`, p_corrected `{python} deg_loc_cset_better_p`), but higher from `{python} deg_loc_cset_worse_start`% on (dz = `{python} deg_loc_cset_worse_dz`, p_corrected `{python} deg_loc_cset_worse_p`).

Spatial correlation followed the same pattern (Annex Figure 8). wCSET's correlation fell from `{python} deg_summary_corr_wcset_0` to `{python} deg_summary_corr_wcset_100`, against `{python} deg_summary_ref_corr_sloreta` for sLORETA. It was significantly higher than sLORETA's up to `{python} deg_corr_wcset_better_end`% (dz = `{python} deg_corr_wcset_better_dz`, p_corrected `{python} deg_corr_wcset_better_p`), and its deficit at 100% was not significant (p_corrected `{python} deg_corr_wcset_worse_p`). CSET's correlation stayed at `{python} deg_summary_corr_cset_lo_s`–`{python} deg_summary_corr_cset_hi_s` up to 60%, then dropped to `{python} deg_summary_corr_cset_100`. It was higher than sLORETA's up to `{python} deg_corr_cset_better_end`% (dz = `{python} deg_corr_cset_better_dz`, p_corrected `{python} deg_corr_cset_better_p`), but lower from `{python} deg_corr_cset_worse_start`% on (dz = `{python} deg_corr_cset_worse_dz`, p_corrected `{python} deg_corr_cset_worse_p`).


### Surrogate alternatives {#sec-s1-surrogates}
```{python filename="simf_surrogate_stats.py"}
#| output: false
import mindmap as mm

# Surrogate connectomes compared with the original.
surrogates = ["beltrami", "fused", "fused-bin", "geom-atlas", "geom-atlas-bin"]
conditions = ["original"] + surrogates

# Display names for the surrogate tags.
SURROGATE_LABELS = {
    "fused": "atlas", "fused-bin": "atlas-bin",
    "geom-atlas": "local", "geom-atlas-bin": "local-bin",
}
methods = ["cset", "wcset"]

# Surrogate vs. original connectome, per method.
surr_metrics = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load("./results/simf/surrogates")
surr_comparisons = surr_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(["original"], surrogates)

# Localization error at qrp, paired by region.
surr_loc_results = {}
for method in methods:
    surr_loc_results[method] = surr_metrics.stat.wilcoxon(
        "localization_error", group_by="Surrogate",
        comparisons=surr_comparisons, pairing_col="region",
        filters={"Method": method, "phase": "qrp"},
    )

# Statistics quoted in the prose.
_loc_wcset = surr_loc_results["wcset"].vs("original")  # effect as stored (original - surrogate)
loc_wcset_p = {s: fmt_p(_loc_wcset.loc[s, "p_corrected"]) for s in surrogates}
loc_wcset_r = {s: fmt_stat(_loc_wcset.loc[s, "effect"]) for s in surrogates}
loc_wcset_r_lo = fmt_stat(_loc_wcset.loc[surrogates, "effect"].abs().min())
loc_wcset_r_hi = fmt_stat(_loc_wcset.loc[surrogates, "effect"].abs().max())

# Spatial correlation at qrp and peak, paired by region.
surr_ref_corr = surr_metrics.metadata["derived"]["ref_corr"]

surr_corr_results = {}
for phase in ["qrp", "pp"]:
    for method in methods:
        surr_corr_results[(method, phase)] = surr_metrics.stat.wilcoxon(
            "correlation", group_by="Surrogate",
            comparisons=surr_comparisons, pairing_col="region",
            filters={"Method": method, "phase": phase},
        )

# Statistics quoted in the prose.
def _corr_row(method, phase, surrogate):
    return surr_corr_results[(method, phase)].vs("original").loc[surrogate].rename({"effect": "effect_size"})

corr_wcset_beltrami_qrp, corr_wcset_beltrami_pp = _corr_row("wcset", "qrp", "beltrami"), _corr_row("wcset", "pp", "beltrami")
corr_wcset_beltrami_r_lo = fmt_stat(min(abs(corr_wcset_beltrami_qrp["effect_size"]), abs(corr_wcset_beltrami_pp["effect_size"])))
corr_wcset_beltrami_r_hi = fmt_stat(max(abs(corr_wcset_beltrami_qrp["effect_size"]), abs(corr_wcset_beltrami_pp["effect_size"])))

corr_wcset_beltrami_qrp_median = fmt_num(surr_metrics.metadata["derived"]["wcset_beltrami_qrp_median"], 2)
corr_wcset_beltrami_pp_median = fmt_num(surr_metrics.metadata["derived"]["wcset_beltrami_pp_median"], 2)
corr_dspm_qrp_ref = fmt_num(surr_ref_corr["qrp"]["dspm"], 2)
corr_dspm_pp_ref = fmt_num(surr_ref_corr["pp"]["dspm"], 2)
corr_sloreta_qrp_ref = fmt_num(surr_ref_corr["qrp"]["sloreta"], 2)
corr_sloreta_pp_ref = fmt_num(surr_ref_corr["pp"]["sloreta"], 2)

corr_wcset_fused_qrp, corr_wcset_fused_pp = _corr_row("wcset", "qrp", "fused"), _corr_row("wcset", "pp", "fused")
corr_wcset_fused_p_qrp, corr_wcset_fused_p_pp = fmt_p(corr_wcset_fused_qrp["p_corrected"]), fmt_p(corr_wcset_fused_pp["p_corrected"])
corr_wcset_fusedbin_qrp, corr_wcset_fusedbin_pp = _corr_row("wcset", "qrp", "fused-bin"), _corr_row("wcset", "pp", "fused-bin")
corr_wcset_fusedbin_p_qrp, corr_wcset_fusedbin_p_pp = fmt_p(corr_wcset_fusedbin_qrp["p_corrected"]), fmt_p(corr_wcset_fusedbin_pp["p_corrected"])
corr_wcset_geom_qrp, corr_wcset_geombin_qrp = _corr_row("wcset", "qrp", "geom-atlas"), _corr_row("wcset", "qrp", "geom-atlas-bin")
corr_wcset_geom_p_qrp = fmt_p(max(corr_wcset_geom_qrp["p_corrected"], corr_wcset_geombin_qrp["p_corrected"]))
corr_wcset_geom_pp, corr_wcset_geombin_pp = _corr_row("wcset", "pp", "geom-atlas"), _corr_row("wcset", "pp", "geom-atlas-bin")
corr_wcset_geom_p_pp = fmt_p(corr_wcset_geom_pp["p_corrected"])
corr_wcset_geombin_p_pp = fmt_p(corr_wcset_geombin_pp["p_corrected"])

# Effect-size ranges quoted in the prose.
_corr_wcset_qrp_abs = [
    abs(corr_wcset_beltrami_qrp["effect_size"]), abs(corr_wcset_fused_qrp["effect_size"]),
    abs(corr_wcset_fusedbin_qrp["effect_size"]), abs(corr_wcset_geom_qrp["effect_size"]),
    abs(corr_wcset_geombin_qrp["effect_size"]),
]
corr_wcset_r_lo_qrp = fmt_stat(min(_corr_wcset_qrp_abs))
corr_wcset_r_hi_qrp = fmt_stat(max(_corr_wcset_qrp_abs))

_corr_wcset_pp_abs = [
    abs(corr_wcset_beltrami_pp["effect_size"]), abs(corr_wcset_fused_pp["effect_size"]),
    abs(corr_wcset_fusedbin_pp["effect_size"]), abs(corr_wcset_geom_pp["effect_size"]),
    abs(corr_wcset_geombin_pp["effect_size"]),
]
corr_wcset_r_lo_pp = fmt_stat(min(_corr_wcset_pp_abs))
corr_wcset_r_hi_pp = fmt_stat(max(_corr_wcset_pp_abs))

# p-values quoted in the prose.
loc_wcset_p_max = f'{_loc_wcset.loc[surrogates, "p_corrected"].max():.3f}'
corr_wcset_p_max_pp = fmt_p(max(_corr_row("wcset", "pp", s)["p_corrected"] for s in surrogates))
_qrp_sig = [s for s in surrogates if _corr_row("wcset", "qrp", s)["p_corrected"] < 0.05]
corr_wcset_n_sig_qrp = len(_qrp_sig)

# CSET, oriented so that positive r = surrogate better. Stored effects are original - surrogate:
# for localization error that is already "positive = surrogate better", for correlation it is flipped.
_cset_r = {("loc", s): r for s, r in surr_loc_results["cset"].vs("original")["effect"].items()}
_cset_p = {("loc", s): p for s, p in surr_loc_results["cset"].vs("original")["p_corrected"].items()}
for _ph in ["qrp", "pp"]:
    _v = surr_corr_results[("cset", _ph)].vs("original")
    _cset_r.update({(_ph, s): -r for s, r in _v["effect"].items()})
    _cset_p.update({(_ph, s): p for s, p in _v["p_corrected"].items()})
cset_beltrami_loc_r = fmt_stat(_cset_r[("loc", "beltrami")])
# Every other significant CSET difference is a small deficit.
_cset_other = [r for k, r in _cset_r.items() if _cset_p[k] < 0.05 and k != ("loc", "beltrami")]
assert all(r < 0 for r in _cset_other)
cset_other_r_lo, cset_other_r_hi = fmt_stat(min(_cset_other)), fmt_stat(max(_cset_other))
```

We replaced the true connectome with the dMRI-free surrogates of @sec-connectome, keeping wCSET's hyperparameters unchanged (@fig-surrogate; Wilcoxon signed-rank vs. the true connectome, region-paired, FDR-corrected; rank-biserial r, positive = surrogate better). wCSET performed better with every surrogate than with the true connectome, and no surrogate stood out from the others. Its localization error was lower with all five surrogates (r = `{python} loc_wcset_r_lo`–`{python} loc_wcset_r_hi`, all p_corrected ≤ `{python} loc_wcset_p_max`). Its spatial correlation was higher with all five at the peak (r = `{python} corr_wcset_r_lo_pp`–`{python} corr_wcset_r_hi_pp`, all p_corrected `{python} corr_wcset_p_max_pp`), and with `{python} corr_wcset_n_sig_qrp` of five at the quarter rising phase, where the effects were small (r = `{python} corr_wcset_r_lo_qrp`–`{python} corr_wcset_r_hi_qrp`). With any surrogate, wCSET's correlation stayed roughly 3–4 times that of dSPM and sLORETA.

CSET changed little: with most surrogates, differences were either not significant or small deficits (r = `{python} cset_other_r_lo` to `{python} cset_other_r_hi`). The exception was the Beltrami surrogate, which markedly worsened its localization (r = `{python} cset_beltrami_loc_r`; full CSET results in Annex Figure 9).

```{python filename="simf_surrogate_plot.py"}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-surrogate
#| fig-cap: "wCSET accuracy using the true structural connectome versus five dMRI-free connectome surrogates (subject sub-10). Column a: localization error at the quarter rising phase; column b: spatial correlation with ground truth at the quarter rising phase; column c: spatial correlation with ground truth at the peak phase. Row 1 (a1, b1, c1): values per connectome condition; row 2 (a2, b2, c2): paired differences vs. the original connectome. (a1, b1, c1) Per condition (box = IQR, line = median); dashed lines mark dSPM's and sLORETA's true-connectome medians as reference. (a2, b2, c2) Paired difference vs. the original connectome for the panel above, one value per region (mean over repetitions; violin = distribution, thick line = median, thin line = IQR), oriented so positive = surrogate better. Above each violin: significance vs. the original connectome (Wilcoxon signed-rank, region-paired, FDR-corrected), rank-biserial r (positive = surrogate better), and the number of regions where the surrogate is better/tied/worse. CSET's equivalent comparisons are reported in Annex Figure 9."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Colors per connectome condition (original = gray).
CONDITION_COLORS = {
    "original": LINE_COLOR,
    "beltrami": "#2a78d6",
    "fused": "#eb6834",
    "fused-bin": "#1baf7a",
    "geom-atlas": "#eda100",
    "geom-atlas-bin": "#e87ba4",
}

surr_ref_loc = surr_metrics.metadata["derived"]["ref_loc"]
ref_methods = ["dspm", "sloreta"]
panel_letters = {"loc": "a1", "qrp": "b1", "pp": "c1"}

def surr_ref_lines(medians):
    """dSPM's and sLORETA's true-connectome medians, drawn as dashed reference lines."""
    return {f"{METHOD_LABELS[m]} (original connectome)": (medians[m], COLORS[m]) for m in ref_methods}

# wCSET only; CSET is in the Annex.
surr_fig, _surr_grid = plt.subplots(
    2, 3, figsize=(len(conditions) * 1.3 * 2.4, 11), gridspec_kw={"hspace": 0.55},
)
surr_axes, surr_daxes = _surr_grid[0], _surr_grid[1]

# (a) Localization error at qrp
ax_loc = surr_axes[0]
surr_metrics.plot.group_comparison(
    surr_loc_results["wcset"], order=conditions, palette=CONDITION_COLORS, points=False, showfliers=False,
    width=0.6, alpha=0, saturation=1, fill_alpha=FILL_ALPHA, tick_labels=SURROGATE_LABELS,
    reference_suffix=" (ref.)", reference_lines=surr_ref_lines(surr_ref_loc), ax=ax_loc,
)
plt.setp(ax_loc.get_xticklabels(), rotation=45, ha="right")
ax_loc.set_xlabel("")
ax_loc.set_ylabel("Localization error (mm)")
ax_loc.set_title(f"{panel_letters['loc']}. Localization error per condition", loc="left", fontsize=10)
ax_loc.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

# (b, c) Spatial correlation at qrp and peak, shared y-scale
corr_axes = {}
for phase in ["qrp", "pp"]:
    ax = surr_axes[1 if phase == "qrp" else 2]
    corr_axes[phase] = ax
    surr_metrics.plot.group_comparison(
        surr_corr_results[("wcset", phase)], order=conditions, palette=CONDITION_COLORS, points=False,
        showfliers=False, width=0.6, alpha=0, saturation=1, fill_alpha=FILL_ALPHA, tick_labels=SURROGATE_LABELS,
        reference_suffix=" (ref.)", reference_lines=surr_ref_lines(surr_ref_corr[phase]), ax=ax,
    )
    plt.setp(ax.get_xticklabels(), rotation=45, ha="right")
    ax.set_xlabel("")
    ax.set_ylabel("Spatial correlation")
    ax.set_title(f"{panel_letters[phase]}. Spatial correlation per condition", loc="left", fontsize=10)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
for ax in corr_axes.values():
    ax.set_ylim(0, 0.9)

# (d–f) Paired differences per region, positive = surrogate better: "original" is the reference,
# so the metric's direction is flipped (higher_is_better=not ...) to orient differences toward the surrogate.
_surr_panels = [
    ("a2", "Localization error", surr_loc_results["wcset"], False, "Original − surrogate\n(localization error, mm)"),
    ("b2", "Spatial correlation", surr_corr_results[("wcset", "qrp")], True, "Surrogate − original\n(spatial correlation)"),
    ("c2", "Spatial correlation", surr_corr_results[("wcset", "pp")], True, "Surrogate − original\n(spatial correlation)"),
]
for i, (dax, (letter, metric_label, res, hib, ylabel)) in enumerate(zip(surr_daxes, _surr_panels)):
    surr_metrics.plot.paired_differences(
        res, reference="original", higher_is_better=not hib, order=surrogates, palette=CONDITION_COLORS,
        annotate=("stars", "effect", "counts"), tick_labels=SURROGATE_LABELS, ax=dax,
        direction_labels=("surrogate better", "original better") if i == len(_surr_panels) - 1 else None,
    )
    plt.setp(dax.get_xticklabels(), rotation=45, ha="right")
    dax.set_ylabel(ylabel)
    dax.set_title(f"{letter}. {metric_label}:\npaired difference vs. original", loc="left", fontsize=10)

surr_fig.legend(*ax_loc.get_legend_handles_labels(), loc="lower center", ncol=2, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.04))

plt.tight_layout()

# Column headers: each column is one metric/phase, per-condition values on top, paired differences below
surr_fig.subplots_adjust(top=0.88)
column_headers(surr_fig, zip(surr_axes, ["LOCALIZATION ERROR\n(quarter rising phase)",
                                        "SPATIAL CORRELATION\n(quarter rising phase)",
                                        "SPATIAL CORRELATION\n(peak phase)"]), y=0.94)
```

## Study II: Clinical Localization (Resection Cohort) {#sec-study2}

### Localization Error {#sec-s2-localization}

```{python filename="results_resection_localization.py"}
#| output: false
import mindmap as mm

# Study II methods: Study I methods plus Beltrami.
RESECTION_METHODS = METHODS + ["beltrami"]

# Resection cohort metrics.
resection_metrics = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load("./results/spike/resection")

# pat01: no usable mask or channel locations; pat18: no resection zone.
EXCLUDED_SUBJECTS = ["pat01", "pat18"]
all_subjects = resection_metrics.to_df(metrics="peak_distance_mm")["Subject"].unique()
included_subjects = [s for s in all_subjects if s not in EXCLUDED_SUBJECTS]

# Seizure-free subjects (ILAE 1), half rising phase.
FILTERS = {"phase": "hrp", "ILAE": 1, "Subject": included_subjects}
resection_n = resection_metrics.metadata["derived"]["resection_n"]

competitors = [m for m in RESECTION_METHODS if m != "wcset"]

# Peak-to-resection distance: wCSET vs. each competitor, paired by subject.
resection_results = {}
resection_results["peak_distance_mm"] = resection_metrics.stat.wilcoxon(
    "peak_distance_mm", group_by="Method",
    comparisons=resection_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(["wcset"], competitors),
    pairing_col="Subject", filters=FILTERS,
)

# Statistics quoted in the prose.
_peak = resection_results["peak_distance_mm"]

_peak_medians = resection_metrics.metadata["derived"]["peak_median"]

resection_peak_median_wcset = fmt_num(_peak_medians["wcset"])
resection_peak_median_cset = fmt_num(_peak_medians["cset"])
resection_peak_median_sloreta = fmt_num(_peak_medians["sloreta"])
resection_peak_median_dspm = fmt_num(_peak_medians["dspm"])
resection_peak_median_wmne = fmt_num(_peak_medians["wmne"])
resection_peak_median_beltrami = fmt_num(_peak_medians["beltrami"])

_peak_vs = _peak.vs("wcset")  # one row per competitor, effect as stored (wCSET - competitor)
resection_peak_p_cset = fmt_p(_peak_vs.loc["cset", "p_corrected"])
resection_peak_r_cset = fmt_stat(_peak_vs.loc["cset", "effect"])
resection_peak_p_dspm = fmt_p(_peak_vs.loc["dspm", "p_corrected"])
resection_peak_r_dspm = fmt_stat(_peak_vs.loc["dspm", "effect"])
resection_peak_p_sloreta = fmt_p(_peak_vs.loc["sloreta", "p_corrected"])
resection_peak_r_sloreta = fmt_stat(_peak_vs.loc["sloreta", "effect"])
resection_peak_p_wmne = fmt_p(_peak_vs.loc["wmne", "p_corrected"])
resection_peak_r_wmne = fmt_stat(_peak_vs.loc["wmne", "effect"])
resection_peak_p_beltrami = fmt_p(_peak_vs.loc["beltrami", "p_corrected"])
resection_peak_r_beltrami = fmt_stat(_peak_vs.loc["beltrami", "effect"])

# Competitor closest to significance, quoted in the prose.
_closest = _peak_vs.loc[competitors, "p_corrected"].idxmin()
resection_peak_closest = METHOD_LABELS[_closest]
resection_peak_p_min = fmt_p(_peak_vs.loc[_closest, "p_corrected"])

# Number of patients whose peak falls inside the resection (distance 0 mm), methods grouped by count.
_inside = (resection_metrics.to_df(metrics="peak_distance_mm", filters=FILTERS)
           .assign(inside=lambda d: d["Value"] == 0).groupby("Method")["inside"].sum())
_groups = [" and ".join(METHOD_LABELS[m] for m in RESECTION_METHODS if _inside[m] == n)
           for n in sorted(_inside.unique(), reverse=True)]
_counts = sorted(_inside.unique(), reverse=True)
resection_inside = ", ".join(f"{n} for {g}" for n, g in zip(_counts[1:-1], _groups[1:-1]))
resection_inside = (f"{_counts[0]} of {resection_n} patients for {_groups[0]}, " + resection_inside
                    + f", and {_counts[-1]} for {_groups[-1]}")

# Effect sizes, flipped so that positive = wCSET better (stored: wCSET - competitor distance).
_r = -_peak_vs.loc[competitors, "effect"]
assert (_r > 0).all()  # the prose says every effect favoured wCSET
resection_r_lo, resection_r_hi = fmt_stat(_r.min()), fmt_stat(_r.max())

# Example subject (fixed in processing_spike.qmd) and how often wCSET's / sLORETA's peaks are inside.
_in = (resection_metrics.to_df(metrics="peak_distance_mm", filters=FILTERS)
       .pivot_table(index="Subject", columns="Method", values="Value") == 0)
resection_both_in = int((_in["wcset"] & _in["sloreta"]).sum())
resection_wcset_only_in = int((_in["wcset"] & ~_in["sloreta"]).sum())
resection_sloreta_only_in = int((~_in["wcset"] & _in["sloreta"]).sum())
```

Simulation offers a controlled testbed, but real clinical data will always differ. We evaluated localization accuracy against the resected epileptogenic zone in seizure-free patients (ILAE 1, n=`{python} resection_n`), comparing wCSET with CSET, wMNE, dSPM, sLORETA, and GBF (@sec-inverse; labelled Beltrami in the figures, after the Laplace-Beltrami eigenmodes it uses).

At the half rising phase (@sec-metric-loc), peak-to-resection distance was lowest for Beltrami and wCSET (@fig-resection-localization a; medians `{python} resection_peak_median_beltrami` and `{python} resection_peak_median_wcset` mm). sLORETA (`{python} resection_peak_median_sloreta` mm), CSET (`{python} resection_peak_median_cset` mm) and wMNE (`{python} resection_peak_median_wmne` mm) followed, and dSPM had the largest median (`{python} resection_peak_median_dspm` mm). The effects all favoured wCSET but none reached significance (Wilcoxon signed-rank, subject-paired, FDR-corrected; rank-biserial r = `{python} resection_r_lo`–`{python} resection_r_hi`, positive = wCSET better), the closest being `{python} resection_peak_closest` (p_corrected `{python} resection_peak_p_min`). The peak fell inside the resection in `{python} resection_inside`.

```{python filename="results_resection_localization_plot.py"}

# (a) Per method
```
