An individual example illustrates what this distance means spatially (@fig-resection-localization b). In this patient, the peaks of both wCSET and sLORETA fall inside the resection at the half rising phase, as in `{python} resection_both_in` of the `{python} resection_n` patients. Only wCSET's peak was inside in `{python} resection_wcset_only_in` others, and only sLORETA's in `{python} resection_sloreta_only_in`.



## Study III: Clinical Dynamics (Simultaneous iEEG/EEG) {#sec-study3}

### Spatial Correlation Analysis

Study II scored a single location per patient. Study III instead tests how well each method reproduces the spatial pattern of activity recorded intracranially, across contacts and over time.

wCSET was compared against every other method at the timepoint level, on two sign-free measures: the amplitude rank correlation and the AUC (@sec-metric-corr, @sec-metric-auc), via the autocorrelation-corrected paired test of @sec-stats.

```{python filename="results_intra_vieeg_significance.py"}
#| output: false
import mindmap as mm
import pandas as pd

# Amplitude rank correlation (Spearman, |amplitude|) and AUC on |amplitude|, per subject, method and timepoint
# (processing_intra.qmd, "Spatial pattern metrics").
SPATIAL_DIR = "./results/intra/spatial_metrics"
vieeg_metrics = mm.metric.MetricSuite.load(SPATIAL_DIR)

# Subjects 12 and 50 (deep sources, far from the cortical source space) are reported in the Annex.
SUBJECT_ORDER = ["34", "48", "12", "50"]
MAIN_SUBJECTS = ["48", "34"]
SUBJECT_TITLES = {
    "34": "Subject 2",
    "48": "Subject 1",
    "12": "sub-12\n(deep source)",
    "50": "sub-50\n(deep source)",
}

# Competitor order matches processing_intra.qmd, whose cached statistics are reused.
COMPETITORS = ["sloreta", "cset", "dspm", "wmne", "beltrami"]
STANDARD = ["cset", "sloreta", "dspm", "wmne"]  # Beltrami reported separately
VIEEG_METRICS = {"correlation_spatial_absrank": "amplitude rank correlation", "auc_spatial": "AUC on |amplitude|"}

# Per-timepoint values and cached test results.
vieeg_wide, vieeg_results = {}, {}
for metric in VIEEG_METRICS:
    for subject in SUBJECT_ORDER:
        wide = (vieeg_metrics.to_df(metrics=metric, filters={"Subject": subject})
                .pivot_table(index="times", columns="Method", values="Value").dropna())
        vieeg_wide[(subject, metric)] = wide
        vieeg_results[(subject, metric)] = vieeg_metrics.stat.ttest_ess(
            metric, group_by="Method", comparisons=vieeg_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(["wcset"], COMPETITORS),
            pairing_col="times", subject_order=wide.index.tolist(), filters={"Subject": subject},
        )

# Statistics quoted in the prose: p-values and effects (positive = wCSET better) per competitor,
# and the per-timepoint differences wCSET - competitor behind each test.
vieeg_vs = {k: r.vs("wcset") for k, r in vieeg_results.items()}
vieeg_diffs = {k: vieeg_metrics.stat.paired_differences(r) for k, r in vieeg_results.items()}

def _median(subject, metric, method):
    return vieeg_wide[(subject, metric)][method].median()

_r, _auc = "correlation_spatial_absrank", "auc_spatial"

# Subject 1: wCSET vs. the four standard methods and CSET, then Beltrami.
_r48, _auc48 = vieeg_vs[("48", _r)], vieeg_vs[("48", _auc)]
_win48 = (vieeg_diffs[("48", _r)] > 0).mean() * 100  # % of timepoints where wCSET is higher
vieeg_48_r_wcset = fmt_num(_median("48", _r, "wcset"), 2)
vieeg_48_r_std_lo = fmt_num(min(_median("48", _r, c) for c in STANDARD), 2)
vieeg_48_r_std_hi = fmt_num(max(_median("48", _r, c) for c in STANDARD), 2)
vieeg_48_r_beltrami = fmt_num(_median("48", _r, "beltrami"), 2)
vieeg_48_spatial_p4_max = fmt_p(_r48.loc[STANDARD, "p_corrected"].max())
vieeg_48_spatial_dz4_lo = fmt_stat(_r48.loc[STANDARD, "effect"].min())
vieeg_48_spatial_dz4_hi = fmt_stat(_r48.loc[STANDARD, "effect"].max())
vieeg_48_winrate_min = f"{_win48[STANDARD].min():.0f}"
vieeg_48_winrate_max = f"{_win48[STANDARD].max():.0f}"
vieeg_48_spatial_p_beltrami = fmt_p(_r48.loc["beltrami", "p_corrected"])
vieeg_48_beltrami_winrate = f"{_win48['beltrami']:.0f}"
vieeg_48_auc_p4_max = fmt_p(_auc48.loc[STANDARD, "p_corrected"].max())
vieeg_48_auc_dz4_lo = fmt_stat(_auc48.loc[STANDARD, "effect"].min())
vieeg_48_auc_dz4_hi = fmt_stat(_auc48.loc[STANDARD, "effect"].max())
vieeg_48_auc_p_beltrami = fmt_p(_auc48.loc["beltrami", "p_corrected"])

# Subject 2: smallest p over every competitor and both metrics.
vieeg_34_p_min = fmt_p(min(vieeg_vs[("34", m)]["p_corrected"].min() for m in VIEEG_METRICS))
vieeg_34_r_wcset = fmt_num(_median("34", _r, "wcset"), 2)
vieeg_34_r_std_lo = fmt_num(min(_median("34", _r, c) for c in STANDARD), 2)
vieeg_34_r_std_hi = fmt_num(max(_median("34", _r, c) for c in STANDARD), 2)

# Signed Pearson correlation (Annex Figure 11), for comparison with Grova et al. 2016 and Afnan et al. 2026.
_signed = "correlation_spatial_signed"
_signed_vs, _signed_wide = {}, {}
for _s in MAIN_SUBJECTS:
    _w = (vieeg_metrics.to_df(metrics=_signed, filters={"Subject": _s})
          .pivot_table(index="times", columns="Method", values="Value").dropna())
    _signed_wide[_s] = _w
    _signed_vs[_s] = vieeg_metrics.stat.ttest_ess(
        _signed, group_by="Method", comparisons=vieeg_metrics.stat.build_comparisons(["wcset"], COMPETITORS),
        pairing_col="times", subject_order=_w.index.tolist(), filters={"Subject": _s},
    ).vs("wcset")
signed_48_wcset = fmt_num(_signed_wide["48"]["wcset"].median(), 2)
signed_48_std_lo = fmt_num(min(_signed_wide["48"][c].median() for c in STANDARD), 2)
signed_48_std_hi = fmt_num(max(_signed_wide["48"][c].median() for c in STANDARD), 2)
signed_48_p_max = fmt_p(_signed_vs["48"].loc[STANDARD, "p_corrected"].max())
signed_48_dz_lo = fmt_stat(_signed_vs["48"].loc[STANDARD, "effect"].min())
signed_48_dz_hi = fmt_stat(_signed_vs["48"].loc[STANDARD, "effect"].max())
signed_34_p_min = fmt_p(_signed_vs["34"]["p_corrected"].min())

# Glass-brain example (processing_intra.qmd): rho and top-contact overlap at the timepoint shown.
import json
_glass = {s_: json.load(open(f"./results/intra/glass_example/sub-{s_}.json")) for s_ in MAIN_SUBJECTS}
glass_n_top = _glass["48"]["n_top"]
glass_48_rho_wcset, glass_48_rho_sloreta = (fmt_num(_glass["48"]["rho"][m], 2) for m in ["wcset", "sloreta"])
glass_34_rho_wcset, glass_34_rho_sloreta = (fmt_num(_glass["34"]["rho"][m], 2) for m in ["wcset", "sloreta"])
glass_34_top_wcset, glass_34_top_sloreta = (_glass["34"]["top_overlap"][m] for m in ["wcset", "sloreta"])
```

In Subject 1 (@fig-intracranial-diff), wCSET's amplitude rank correlation with the recording was significantly higher than that of sLORETA, dSPM, wMNE, and CSET (largest p_corrected `{python} vieeg_48_spatial_p4_max`, dz = `{python} vieeg_48_spatial_dz4_lo`–`{python} vieeg_48_spatial_dz4_hi`), with wCSET higher at `{python} vieeg_48_winrate_min`–`{python} vieeg_48_winrate_max`% of timepoints (median ρ = `{python} vieeg_48_r_wcset`, against `{python} vieeg_48_r_std_lo` to `{python} vieeg_48_r_std_hi` for these four methods). The AUC led to the same conclusion (largest p_corrected `{python} vieeg_48_auc_p4_max`, dz = `{python} vieeg_48_auc_dz4_lo`–`{python} vieeg_48_auc_dz4_hi`). Against Beltrami (median ρ = `{python} vieeg_48_r_beltrami`), neither metric differed significantly (rank correlation p_corrected `{python} vieeg_48_spatial_p_beltrami`, AUC p_corrected `{python} vieeg_48_auc_p_beltrami`; wCSET higher at `{python} vieeg_48_beltrami_winrate`% of timepoints).

Subject 2 did not reproduce this pattern: wCSET did not differ significantly from any other method on either metric (smallest p_corrected `{python} vieeg_34_p_min`; median ρ = `{python} vieeg_34_r_wcset` for wCSET, `{python} vieeg_34_r_std_lo` to `{python} vieeg_34_r_std_hi` for the four other methods).

For comparison with @grova_intracranial_2016 and @afnan_assessing_2026, who report the signed Pearson correlation across contacts, we also computed that measure (Annex Figure 11). In Subject 1, it separated wCSET from sLORETA, dSPM, wMNE, and CSET more clearly than the polarity-invariant measures did (median r = `{python} signed_48_wcset`, against `{python} signed_48_std_lo` to `{python} signed_48_std_hi`; dz = `{python} signed_48_dz_lo`–`{python} signed_48_dz_hi`, largest p_corrected `{python} signed_48_p_max`). In Subject 2, it again showed no significant difference (smallest p_corrected `{python} signed_34_p_min`).


```{python filename="results_intra_vieeg_significance_plot.py"}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-intracranial-diff
#| fig-cap: "Spatial agreement between virtual and recorded iEEG, for the two subjects with superficial sources (sub-12/sub-50, with deep sources, are reported in Annex Figure 10). One column per subject (a, b). (a1, b1) Amplitude rank correlation per method at each timepoint of the comparison window: Spearman ρ across contacts between the recorded and the virtual absolute amplitude (box = IQR, line = median, outliers hidden); dotted line = 0. (a2, b2) Paired difference in amplitude rank correlation, wCSET minus each other method, one value per timepoint (violin = distribution, thick line = median, thin line = IQR); positive = wCSET better. (a3, b3) Same paired difference for the AUC on |amplitude|, whether the virtual iEEG places its largest amplitudes on the contacts most active in the recording (active = at least 30% of the recorded maximum; 0.5 = chance). Both measures ignore the sign of the contacts. Above each violin: significance from a paired t-test with an autocorrelation-corrected effective sample size (FDR-corrected; *p<0.05, **p<0.01, ***p<0.001), Cohen's dz (positive = wCSET better; unbounded, unlike the rank-biserial r of the other figures), and the percentage of timepoints at which wCSET's value exceeds the other method's, relative to 50% chance (e.g. +17%: wCSET higher at 67% of timepoints)."
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

VIEEG_ORDER = ["wcset"] + COMPETITORS

# Main-text subjects only; 12 and 50 are in the Annex.
vieeg_fig, vieeg_axes = plt.subplots(
    3, len(MAIN_SUBJECTS), figsize=(4.6 * len(MAIN_SUBJECTS), 12),
    gridspec_kw={"hspace": 0.6, "wspace": 0.3}, squeeze=False,
)
for col_i, subject in enumerate(MAIN_SUBJECTS):
    letter = "ab"[col_i]

    # (1) Spatial correlation per method, chance range shaded
    ax = vieeg_axes[0, col_i]
    vieeg_metrics.plot.group_comparison(
        vieeg_results[(subject, _r)], order=VIEEG_ORDER, palette=COLORS, points=False, showfliers=False, width=0.55,
        alpha=0, saturation=1, fill_alpha=FILL_ALPHA, chance_value=0,
        tick_labels=METHOD_LABELS, reference_suffix=" (ref.)", ax=ax,
    )
    plt.setp(ax.get_xticklabels(), rotation=45, ha="right", fontsize=8)
    ax.set_xlabel("")
    ax.set_ylabel("Amplitude rank correlation (ρ)\nvirtual vs. recorded iEEG" if col_i == 0 else "", fontsize=8)
    ax.set_title(f"{letter}1. {SUBJECT_TITLES[subject]}: amplitude rank correlation per method", loc="left", fontsize=9)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)

    # (2, 3) Paired differences per timepoint, positive = wCSET better
    for row_i, metric in enumerate(VIEEG_METRICS, start=1):
        dax = vieeg_axes[row_i, col_i]
        vieeg_metrics.plot.paired_differences(
            vieeg_results[(subject, metric)], reference="wcset", order=COMPETITORS, palette=COLORS,
            annotate=("stars", "effect", "winrate"), tick_labels=METHOD_LABELS, ax=dax,
            direction_labels=("wCSET better", "other method better") if col_i == len(MAIN_SUBJECTS) - 1 else None,
        )
        plt.setp(dax.get_xticklabels(), rotation=45, ha="right", fontsize=8)
        dax.set_title(f"{letter}{row_i + 1}. {SUBJECT_TITLES[subject]}: {VIEEG_METRICS[metric]},\n"
                      "paired difference vs. wCSET", loc="left", fontsize=9)
        if col_i == 0:
            dax.set_ylabel(f"wCSET − method\n({VIEEG_METRICS[metric]})", fontsize=8)
share_ylim(vieeg_axes[0])  # per-method row comparable across subjects
```

@fig-intra-reconstruction shows one timepoint in detail: the peak of the virtual iEEG's global field power (GFP), averaged over the two methods. In Subject 1, wCSET and sLORETA both placed their largest amplitudes on the same left temporal electrode shafts as the recording, but mostly not on the same contacts within them (ρ = `{python} glass_48_rho_wcset` and `{python} glass_48_rho_sloreta`). In Subject 2, wCSET's largest amplitudes fell on the electrode shaft that dominated the recording, sharing `{python} glass_34_top_wcset` of its `{python} glass_n_top` strongest contacts, against `{python} glass_34_top_sloreta` for sLORETA (ρ = `{python} glass_34_rho_wcset` and `{python} glass_34_rho_sloreta`).

```{python filename="results_intra_spatial_plot.py"}
#| echo: false
#| label: fig-intra-reconstruction
#| fig-cap: "Recorded vs. virtual intracranial EEG at one timepoint, for the two main-text subjects (one row each). (a1, b1) Intracranial global field power (GFP, standard deviation across contacts) of the recorded iEEG and of wCSET's and sLORETA's virtual iEEG, each scaled to its own maximum within the spike window (shaded); the dashed line marks the timepoint shown on the right, the peak of the two virtual GFPs averaged. (a2–a4, b2–b4) Superior view of a translucent cortex with every intracranial contact colored by the rank of its absolute amplitude at that timepoint, from the weakest (0) to the strongest (1) contact of each map: recorded iEEG, wCSET's and sLORETA's virtual iEEG. ρ = amplitude rank correlation with the recording at that timepoint."
import json
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# Glass-brain renders and GFP curves from processing_intra.qmd
GLASS_DIR = "./results/intra/glass_example"
GLASS_METHODS = ["wcset", "sloreta"]
glass = {sub: json.load(open(f"{GLASS_DIR}/sub-{sub}.json")) for sub in MAIN_SUBJECTS}

# sLORETA's GFP fluctuates a lot: thin and behind, so wCSET vs. recorded stays readable
GFP_STYLES = {
    "recorded": dict(color="black", linewidth=1.8, zorder=3, label="Recorded iEEG"),
    "wcset": dict(color=COLORS["wcset"], linewidth=1.4, zorder=2, label="wCSET virtual iEEG"),
    "sloreta": dict(color=COLORS["sloreta"], linewidth=0.7, alpha=0.6, zorder=1, label="sLORETA virtual iEEG"),
}

glass_fig = plt.figure(figsize=(14, 7.6))
_glass_grid = glass_fig.add_gridspec(len(MAIN_SUBJECTS), 4, width_ratios=[1.5, 1, 1, 1], wspace=0.08, hspace=0.35)
for row, sub in enumerate(MAIN_SUBJECTS):
    g = glass[sub]
    letter = "ab"[row]

    # (1) GFP, chosen timepoint marked
    ax = glass_fig.add_subplot(_glass_grid[row, 0])
    ax.axvspan(*g["window"], color="#f1f0eb", zorder=0, linewidth=0)
    for k, style in GFP_STYLES.items():
        ax.plot(g["times"], g["gfp"][k], **style)
    ax.axvline(g["time"], color="#0b0b0b", linestyle="--", linewidth=1)
    ax.text(g["time"], 1.02, f" t = {g['time'] * 1000:.0f} ms", transform=ax.get_xaxis_transform(),
            fontsize=8, ha="left", va="bottom")
    ax.set_ylim(0, 1.05)
    ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
    ax.set_ylabel("Intracranial GFP\n(scaled to own max)")
    ax.set_title(f"{letter}1. {SUBJECT_TITLES[sub]}: intracranial GFP", loc="left", fontsize=10, pad=14)
    ax.spines[["top", "right"]].set_visible(False)
    if row == 0:
        glass_fig.legend(*ax.get_legend_handles_labels(), loc="upper center", ncol=3, fontsize=9,
                         frameon=False, bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, 1.0))

    # (2-4) Glass brains at that timepoint
    for col, k in enumerate(["recorded"] + GLASS_METHODS, start=1):
        ax = glass_fig.add_subplot(_glass_grid[row, col])
        image_panel(ax, f"{GLASS_DIR}/sub-{sub}_{k}.png")
        title = "Recorded iEEG" if k == "recorded" else f"{METHOD_LABELS[k]} virtual iEEG\nρ = {g['rho'][k]:.2f}"
        ax.set_title(f"{letter}{col + 1}. {title}", loc="left", fontsize=10)

# Shared colorbar for every glass brain
_g0 = glass[MAIN_SUBJECTS[0]]
colorbar(glass_fig, [0.62, 0.05, 0.22, 0.012], tuple(_g0["clim"]), _g0["cmap"],
         "Rank of contact |amplitude| at t (0 = weakest, 1 = strongest)")
plt.show()
```

# Discussion

## Simulation Insights

Our connectome-driven propagation model lets a focal source recruit distant regions directly through long-range tracts rather than only spreading through neighbors step by step — a mechanism unavailable to nearest-neighbor spread, and impractical to reproduce with neural mass models at realistic dipole counts [@sanz-leon_mathematical_2015; @nunez_multi-scale_2019] (design rationale in Annex). Because the scalp signal sums every active dipole while the source's own amplitude decays with distance from the origin, the EEG peak systematically lags true onset — consistent with the clinical literature on interictal spike propagation [@vorderwulbecke_high-density_2020; @carboni_linear_2022], and the reason the field localizes on the rising phase rather than at the peak. Within it, we chose the quarter rising phase for simulation, where onset is known exactly and the source is still focal.

At that early, focal point, wCSET localized about as accurately as CSET and dSPM and clearly outperformed wMNE, with a more modest advantage over sLORETA; with 100 regions behind each comparison, effect sizes rather than p-values separate these meaningful and negligible gaps. This is expected: connectivity information should help least while a source is still genuinely focal. Its role becomes clear once the source spreads: spatial correlation with ground truth improves for every method toward the peak, but far more for wCSET and CSET, consistent with the connectome-spectrum representation becoming more compact as activity spreads across the cortex [@rue-queralt_connectome_2021]. This advantage held broadly across single-trial SNR, and, under connectome degradation, wCSET's edge over sLORETA never reversed even under full (100%) edge permutation, unlike CSET's, which reversed into a deficit beyond 80% — a reassuring margin given how much false-positive structure real tractography can contain [@maier-hein_challenge_2017]. This robustness also guided wCSET's own design: an initial attempt to weight harmonics by robustness to perturbation itself [@sipes_integrative_2024] favored both very low- and very high-frequency harmonics, but the latter introduced reconstruction artifacts, leaving the smooth, low-frequency-favoring exponential decay that became wCSET.

That tolerance extended to a more radical test: substituting the true connectome for cheap, dMRI-free surrogates — an atlas prior, a local-geometry rule, or Laplace-Beltrami eigenmodes — left wCSET's accuracy unchanged or slightly improved, with binarized and weighted variants performing almost identically, indicating the benefit rests on topology rather than precise edge weights.

We hypothesize the true connectome's underperformance relative to its surrogates comes down to how spatially concentrated each connectome's harmonics are (inverse participation ratio; Annex Figure 2). The true connectome's harmonics cluster tightly on small, sometimes disjoint groups of dipoles, while the surrogates' harmonics spread more uniformly across the cortex. Because wCSET's weighting forces the reconstruction to lean on these harmonics, a tightly clustered harmonic is a strong, specific bet: it pays off when the signal is clustered similarly, but backfires when the signal is elsewhere — the same trade-off behind the reconstruction artifacts from very high-frequency (most spatially focal) harmonics noted above.

What matters may be less whether a connectome is anatomically *true* than whether its harmonics are spatially homogeneous — explaining why a purely geometric surrogate like Beltrami, which discards white matter connectivity entirely, still reconstructs well: its harmonics are meaningfully less localized than the true connectome's. This points to a specific limitation in how wCSET uses connectivity, not a shortcoming of connectivity information itself: its harmonic weighting has no way to tell whether a cluster it leans on reflects genuinely correlated activity, or is just an artifact of the graph's structure. CSET shows no comparable benefit from these surrogates, consistent with this account: its adaptive, $l_1$-sparse selection of harmonics, rather than wCSET's fixed weighting, means it is never forced to rely on any one harmonic's localization, so it has nothing to be rescued from.

## Epilepsy with Resected Ground Truth

The resection cohort confirmed the simulation's main localization finding: wCSET localized as accurately as every other method. Its peak-to-resection distance was among the lowest, on par with Beltrami, and did not differ significantly from any of the five other methods. Using the same resection cohort, @wang_geometry_2026 report a similar parity for their geometry-only GBF method, with no significant advantage over dSPM, sLORETA, or eLORETA (P = 0.079–0.133). Unlike wCSET here, however, GBF did improve significantly over MNE (P = 0.012). However, localization error was considerably worse here than in simulation. The evaluation point does not explain this gap: although this cohort was evaluated at the half rising phase rather than the simulation's quarter rising phase, re-evaluating it at the quarter rising phase yielded the same pattern of results (Annex), suggesting propagation already underway by the half rising phase is not the main cause. The gap more likely reflects how real recordings differ from our simulation: our simulated noise model may underestimate real physiological noise, and this cohort's reconstructions lacked noise whitening (@sec-data-resection) and relied on an atlas rather than an individual connectome. We included this cohort because localization against a resected ground truth is how the field conventionally validates these methods, and we wanted to confirm wCSET does not perform worse in this more realistic, noisier scenario: its connectivity-informed prior did not trade away localization accuracy for its propagation-tracking advantage.

## Epilepsy with Intracranial Electrodes

As in simulation, we expected wCSET's overall spatial-correlation advantage over standard methods to be higher. Real intracranial recordings confirmed this in one of the two evaluable subjects with a scalp-visible spike, but not the other. In the first, wCSET significantly outperformed sLORETA, dSPM, wMNE, and CSET, on the signed spatial correlation and on the sign-free AUC alike. In the second, it matched every one of them. In neither subject did wCSET perform significantly worse than any other method: it was always as good, or substantially better.

Against Beltrami, neither method came out significantly ahead in either subject. This parity, not a loss, is further evidence that a purely geometric account can rival a connectome-informed one. Using resected epileptogenic zones as ground truth in 20 drug-resistant epilepsy patients, @siu_structural_2026 found the same parity: geometric and connectome eigenmodes performed comparably, with geometric eigenmodes showing only a modest edge in recall.

The remaining two subjects had deep sources invisible on scalp EEG, where no method reconstructed the intracranial signal well. @grova_intracranial_2016 report the same limitation. This is consistent with our framework's reliance on a fixed-orientation, cortically-constrained source model, which cannot properly represent deeper generators. Extending it to such sources would require encoding source orientation within the connectivity structure itself, which we leave for future work.


## Limitations

Our source model has a structural limitation: dipoles are restricted to a fixed-orientation, cortically-constrained grid (@sec-source-space), which excludes deep, subcortical generators entirely. This is a missed opportunity, since tractography, the very data our connectivity prior draws on, also encodes connections to and among deep structures. Relatedly, our surrogate and binarization results (@sec-s1-surrogates) suggest wCSET currently draws its benefit mostly from connectome topology rather than precise edge weights, so the richer, weighted connectivity information remains largely unexploited.

Our regularization parameter ($\lambda_2$) is likewise fixed by an SNR-derived heuristic (@sec-lambda) rather than validated per subject or method, and a post hoc check against the intracranial cohort suggests this matters. Sweeping $\lambda_2$ against that ground truth shows the correlation-maximizing value differs by roughly an order of magnitude across our four subjects, with no single value optimal for all of them. We also checked whether two classical regularization diagnostics that do not require ground truth, the L-curve and generalized cross-validation, could recover a good value without it; neither did. Generalized cross-validation consistently favored several orders of magnitude more regularization than the ground truth confirms is useful, and the L-curve had no genuine corner for this operator, its curvature-based selection instead tracking the degenerate limit where the source estimate collapses to zero. Principled, ground-truth-free selection of $\lambda_2$ therefore remains unsolved for this method, and, more broadly, for any inverse method applied where no ground truth exists to validate against.

We also restricted our standard baselines to methods available in MNE-Python. This excludes LORETA and LAURA, the two algorithms @carboni_linear_2022 found most accurate for interictal spike localization, outperforming sLORETA, eLORETA. It also excludes beamformer methods entirely. A more complete comparison against these alternatives is left for future work.

Our simulation also idealizes several aspects of real recordings: it assumes known conductivities, is built around a single representative subject, and uses propagation and noise models that, while physiologically motivated, remain simplified. Many of its parameters were fixed rather than systematically swept, and some of the effect sizes we report are small enough that different choices could plausibly shift specific comparisons. We remain confident in the broader pattern: spatial correlation improves more for wCSET as a source spreads. But that confidence is only as strong as the simulation's own modeling choices, which may still deviate from real cortical dynamics in ways we cannot yet quantify.

Finally, the intracranial cohort's evaluable sample (two subjects with a scalp-visible spike) is too small to draw firm conclusions from. Even after correcting each subject's own effective sample size for autocorrelation across channels and timepoints, this precludes any statistical test across independent subjects. More subjects are needed before we can be confident these patterns generalize.

# Conclusion

Source reconstruction is conventionally benchmarked on localizing a single, focal generator, a criterion that says little about a method's ability to capture distributed, network-level dynamics. We hypothesized connectivity-informed approaches would be better suited to this, and introduced wCSET, a smooth, exponentially decaying L2 prior over the connectome-harmonic spectrum, to test it directly. We validated wCSET, alongside CSET, three connectivity-agnostic methods, and a geometry-based (Laplace-Beltrami) alternative, against three independent ground truths spanning a source's onset and its distributed activity: simulated connectome propagation, a resected epileptogenic zone, and simultaneous intracranial recordings.

wCSET matched standard methods at localizing a source's onset, including a significant edge over wMNE in simulation. It reconstructed the source's subsequent spread substantially better wherever we could test it directly, beating every connectivity-agnostic method and CSET in simulation, and standard methods and CSET in one of two evaluable intracranial subjects. This advantage held under sensor noise, substantial connectome degradation, and when the true connectome was replaced by simple, dMRI-free surrogates, indicating it rests on coarse, large-scale structure rather than precise individual tractography. The clearest exception was Beltrami: a purely geometric alternative that tracked wCSET's performance throughout and matched it in the resection cohort and against real intracranial recordings, a pattern two independent groups reported in their own geometry-versus-connectome comparisons.

Beyond wCSET itself, we see the three-part validation framework as this work's more durable contribution: simulated, resected, and intracranial ground truths that jointly probe a source's full activity pattern rather than its onset alone. Two pieces of it stand on their own: a connectome-driven propagation simulation that models network-level spread directly in dipole space rather than growing a single patch, and simultaneous EEG/iEEG recordings that validate reconstruction beyond localization entirely. Extending both to future connectivity- and geometry-informed methods, and to source models representing deep and multi-generator activity, are natural next steps toward source imaging that reflects the brain's network organization rather than collapsing it back to a single point.
